key_insight: Cap-and-Track adapts LLM inference dispatch to changing serving capacity instead of relying on a fixed request rate. Backend refusals act as feedback about how much work the system can currently admit.
problem_solved: Fixed dispatch rates become outdated as GPU fleets resize, shared provider capacity fluctuates, and request sizes vary. Unknown output lengths make inference demand difficult to predict at admission time.
method: Use backend refusal signals to track the current admission ceiling and adjust dispatch accordingly.
Hold excess work in durable priority queues rather than immediately sending it to constrained backends.
Support asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs; Meta implements the design in its traffic shaper for post and live-video understanding.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the design offers a way to align asynchronous inference traffic with fluctuating capacity while preserving queued work and its priorities. The supplied abstract is truncated and provides no quantitative performance results.
visual_elements: Flow diagram: incoming requests → durable priority queues → adaptive dispatcher → provider pools and internal GPUs.
Feedback loop showing backend refusals informing dispatch adjustments.
Conceptual time-series chart contrasting a stale fixed dispatch rate with dispatch that follows shifting capacity.
Variable-length request icons illustrating why request count alone does not predict inference demand.
paper_title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
paper_authors: Benjamin Novotny, Doug Szeto, Chang Wang, Shicheng Chen, George Zhihua Yuan
